source_title: Woman living on $300 a month in Nepal buys $170k Yorkshire home at 25
source_excerpt: If you've ever dreamt about owning a home at a young age, you know seeing this dream through can take years of planning, financial commitments and balancing your career alongside it all. If you're young, building your own home could mean balancing a lot. So, while this journey towards owning property takes a conventional route for some, others may find themselves arriving at it through circumstances they may never have imagined.As reported by The Sun, for 25-year-old Madeleine Jaye, it was a rather unconventional route. Her decision to move away from the life she had once planned brought her to an unexpected milestone, allowing her to purchase a Â£170,000 property in Yorkshire while spending much of her time in a small village in Nepal.Hailing from Nottingham, Madeleine had spent four years studying law at Sheffield, with ambitions of securing a position at a major law firm. However, a trip to Nepal introduced her to Ram, her now-husband, who fortuitously changed the course of her life. The two met during a momo cooking class while she was travelling in the country, and what began as an encounter during her travels eventually developed into a relationship that would see her divide her time between two very different parts of the world.Furthermore, according to the report, Madeleine has been living between Britain and Nepal since 2024, when she finished her legal studies. She now spends extended periods in a small village approximately 25 minutes from Pokhara, where she lives with Ram, away from the familiar conveniences of modern British households. Their home does not have hot water, a refrigerator or a washing machine, and the couple prepare their meals over an open fire, making everyday routines considerably different from those she might once have expected.A different approach to living and savingWhat makes Madeleine's story particularly interesting from a property perspective is the way her living arrangements have influenced her ability to save. While the couple's household in Nepal has considerably lower expenses than a typical British household, her financial circumstances are also shaped by the work she continues to undertake in the UK.Madeleine runs her own personal assistant business, providing live-in care and assistance. Her work involves placements in Britain that generally last between six and 12 weeks, with accommodation included, after which she takes a similar period away to spend time with her husband in Nepal. This arrangement allows her to continue earning in Britain without having to maintain the same level of everyday expenditure throughout the year.As reported by The Sun, Madeleine estimates that her monthly expenditure in Nepal is around Â£300 at most. Together, these circumstances have helped her keep her outgoings relatively modest while continuing to work for part of the year.Life beyond the comforts of a modern homeThe lower cost of living, however, comes with its own adjustments. Living close to the natural world means that the surrounding wildlife is not simply something encountered during an occasional trip outdoors. Madeleine has spoken about keeping goats and chickens indoors at night because of the threat posed by tigers, while several animals in the village, including two of their pet dogs, have been lost.The monsoon season brings another set of challenges, making the experience of rural living different from the quieter days the couple otherwise enjoy. Yet Madeleine has come to appreciate the rhythm of life in the village, where swimming, fishing, drinking tea and travelling into the mountains form part of their everyday activities. Speaking about her experience, Madeleine described how living in Nepal had brought her a sense of contentment she had not anticipated. "Spirituality is woven into everyday life," she said, adding that the experience had changed her in ways she had never expected.Rethinking what owning a home and building a life meanMadeleine's decision to move away from her original professional ambitions was also influenced by a deeply personal experience. After losing her father to cancer at the age of 54, she began reconsidering the importance she had once placed on career progression, financial success and the expectations that often accompany them. She has spoken about how his death made her realise that time was considerably more valuable than the conventional idea of success she had grown up with.But this does not mean she has forgotten her interest in pursuing law. She believes she may return to law one day, but for now, her work in Britain and her life in Nepal allow her to maintain a balance that she is comfortable with.
